topics.title: Prompt injection and tool safety
topics.brief: Any text the model reads can contain instructions, so an agent that reads untrusted content and can reach private data or act outside can be steered by an attacker, and no filter fixes this completely.
points: Direct versus indirect: direct injection is a user typing instructions to override the system prompt. Indirect injection hides instructions in content the model reads later, such as a web page, an email, a PDF or a tool result. Indirect is the dangerous one for agents.

Why it works: the model sees one stream of tokens and cannot reliably tell your instructions from instructions that arrived inside data. It resembles SQL injection, except there is no parameterized query to fix it.
The lethal trifecta (Simon Willison): access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out. An agent with all three can be told to leak the data. Remove one leg.

Meta's Rule of Two: in one session an agent should have at most two of untrusted input, access to sensitive data or systems, and the ability to change state or communicate externally. If a task needs all three, add supervision such as human approval.

Defences that stack: least privilege on tools, labelling retrieved text as data, validating output in code, blocking known exfiltration routes, human approval for high-risk actions and red-team testing. Classifiers help but are not a guarantee.
Design for failure: assume some injections succeed. Ask what is the worst action this agent could be talked into, then make that action impossible, not only unlikely.
production: Per Microsoft's security blog on indirect prompt injection, defences are layered: hardened prompts, Spotlighting to mark untrusted text, Prompt Shields classifiers, permissions and sensitivity labels, deterministic blocking of known exfiltration routes, and user approval before risky actions.

Per Anthropic's research post on browser-agent defences, they train against simulated injections, scan untrusted content with classifiers and red-team continuously, and still report a 1.4% attack success rate for their best model against an adaptive attacker, which they call meaningful risk.
Per Simon Willison's lethal trifecta post, the pattern has shown up in real products, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub's MCP server and GitLab Duo.
mine: WheelPrice: the fitment assistant was a constrained agent with four tools only, so what it could do was bounded by the tool set.
In his own words on LLM limits: text the model reads can contain instructions, so retrieved content is treated as data and tools only get the access they need.

95% is so high it will block real users

A longer system prompt would be strictly better

mcq.q: Which change most reduces the damage of a successful injection into a support agent?

Make the system prompt longer

mcq.why: Limiting what the agent can do bounds the worst case, whatever the model reads. The other options do not change what is possible.

open.q: What is prompt injection, and how would you defend an agent against it?
open.probe: That you know indirect injection and design around it instead of relying on filters.
a: Direct injection is a user overriding the rules; indirect hides instructions in content the agent reads: emails, pages, tool results.
The root cause: one stream of tokens, no reliable boundary between instructions and data.
Frame it with the trifecta: private data, untrusted content, a way out; remove one, or limit the agent to two of the three.
Layers: least privilege, retrieved text treated as data, output checked in code, human approval for high-risk actions, red teaming.
Admit it is unsolved: even well-defended systems report a small attack success rate, so limit the blast radius.

say: Prompt injection is when text the model reads contains instructions, and the model follows them. The direct version is a user telling it to ignore its rules. The one that worries me is indirect: the instructions sit inside an email, a web page or a tool result that the agent reads on its own. The model gets one stream of text and can't reliably tell your instructions from instructions that came in as data, so there's no clean fix like parameterized queries for SQL.

So I don't try to win with detection alone. I ask what the agent could be talked into doing, and I limit it. Tools get only the access they need, retrieved content is treated as data, outputs are checked in code, and anything with real consequences gets a person's approval first. Simon Willison's trifecta is a good test: private data, untrusted content, and a way to send data out. If an agent has all three, take one away. At WheelPrice the fitment assistant had four tools and nothing else, so the worst it could do was bounded by design. Filters help, but even the best-defended systems report a small attack success rate, so I design as if some injections get through.
avoid: Saying a system prompt that tells the model to ignore malicious instructions is the defence.
Claiming a filter or classifier solves it: say it is one layer and the damage must be bounded by permissions.
Describing a safety mechanism as if you built it when you only know it from industry practice.

modules.title: 5. Evaluation and validation
modules.blurb: How you know AI output is right: checks in code, a judge you have calibrated, a test set you run on every change, and signals from live traffic.

topics.title: Checking AI output
topics.brief: Treat model output as untrusted input: check what code can check, use a calibrated judge for the rest, and put a person on the output that matters.
points: Untrusted until checked: a model writes text that looks right whether or not it is, so its output is input from a stranger. Validate it before anything downstream acts on it.

Structure first: ask for JSON that matches a schema, parse it, validate it, and on failure feed the error back for a bounded number of retries, then fail cleanly. Strict structured output from the provider removes most parse failures.
Structure is not truth: a reply can match the schema and still name an order that does not exist. Schema checks catch the shape, so ids, numbers and claims are checked against the source of truth.

Cheapest check first: schema, then rules and lookups, then a model judge for what code cannot decide (is this claim supported, is this reply on topic), then a person. Each layer costs more and catches different failures.
Make claims checkable: have the model cite the passage behind each claim, then verify the citation in code. A claim with no supporting quote is removed.
Generated code is output too: run the tests and read the diff. 'All tests pass' from an agent is a claim, not evidence, so ask for the command and its real output.
production: Per OpenAI's Structured Outputs guide, a strict JSON Schema makes responses adhere to the schema, and a safety refusal arrives as a separate field that your code must check before parsing.

Per AWS's documentation, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails has a contextual grounding check that scores each response for grounding in the source and relevance to the query, and filters responses below thresholds you set.
Per Anthropic's guide to reducing hallucinations, you can have Claude find a supporting quote for each claim after it answers and retract any claim it cannot support.
mine: MockFlow-AI: an LLM scores five competencies with cited evidence, and the final hiring verdict is computed in code, not by the model.
alfred_ (5,000+ active users): the eval harness I built from scratch scores with hybrid deterministic plus LLM-as-judge checks.

open.q: How do you validate AI output before you trust it?
open.probe: Thoughtful, not blind, use of AI: layers of checks, and what you do for generated code.
a: Code checks first: a schema, ids that must exist, numbers that must match the source, tests that must pass.
Then a judge for what code cannot decide, such as whether a claim is supported by the source.
Calibrate that judge against a small human-labelled gold set and report an agreement number.
Consequential output gets a person's approval before it takes effect.
An example with a number: MockFlow-AI, evidence-cited scores, a verdict computed in code, weighted kappa 0.82 on a 50-item gold set.

say: Whatever can be checked in code, I check in code: the output matches a schema, the ids it mentions exist, the numbers match the source, and for code, the tests pass and I've read the diff. That catches the cheap failures without trusting anything. A schema only tells me the shape is right, not that the values are, so I always check those against the source.

For the things code can't decide, like whether a claim is actually supported, I use a judge, a second model with a rubric, but I don't trust the judge either until I've measured it against people. In MockFlow-AI I built an LLM-as-judge for interview verdicts: it had to cite evidence for each of five competencies, the final verdict was computed deterministically from those scores, and I calibrated it against a 50-item human gold set, weighted kappa 0.82. And anything with real consequences gets a human approval before it happens.
avoid: Treating a passing schema check as proof the answer is true.
Using a second model to check everything, including what a lookup in code would settle for free.
Letting a retry loop run without a limit.

topics.title: LLM-as-judge and calibration
topics.brief: A model grades another model's output against a rubric, which scales review past what people can read, but it is a measuring instrument and has to be checked against people.
points: Three shapes: score one answer against a rubric, pick the better of two answers (pairwise), or compare with a reference answer. Pairwise is steadier for subjective quality; direct scoring suits clear criteria.
Make the rubric binary and specific: 'is every claim supported by the context? PASS or FAIL with one sentence of reason' beats 'rate the quality from 1 to 10', which drifts and bunches in the middle.

Known biases: position (prefers the first answer), verbosity (prefers the longer one) and self-preference (prefers its own model family). Swap the order, average, and keep only verdicts that survive the swap.

Calibrate against people: they label a gold set, the judge labels the same items, you measure agreement. Use Cohen's kappa, kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e), because it removes the agreement you would get by chance. A judge that always says PASS scores well on raw agreement when most items pass.
Reading kappa: roughly 0.61 to 0.80 is substantial and above 0.80 is almost perfect. For an ordered scale use weighted kappa, which counts a miss by three points as worse than a miss by one.

Keep it honest after launch: look at recall on the failures people found, not only the average; freeze the gold set; and re-run it whenever the judge model or the rubric changes. Never give the judge what code can decide.
production: In the LMSYS paper on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (Zheng et al., 2023), GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time, the same level as humans agree with each other, and the authors document position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases.
Per Anthropic's engineering post on evals for agents, model-based graders handle open-ended output but are non-deterministic, and they are calibrated against human graders.

Verbosity bias: ask for longer answers

It counts every disagreement equally
It penalises a miss by one point less than a miss by four, which fits an ordered scale
It removes chance agreement, which plain kappa does not
It only works with two categories

open.q: Can you trust an LLM judge? How would you check?
open.probe: Whether you know the biases and how to measure agreement, with a real number.
a: Not by default: a judge is a measuring instrument and has to be checked.
Keep the job small: a specific binary rubric with a one-line reason, and know the biases (position, length, own model family).
Calibrate: people label a gold set, the judge labels the same items, measure kappa rather than raw agreement, and look at recall on failures.
An example: MockFlow-AI, evidence-cited scoring, 50-item human gold set, weighted kappa 0.82.
Re-check when the judge model or rubric changes, and never give the judge what code can decide.

say: I wouldn't trust one by default. A judge is a measuring instrument, so I check it the way I'd check any instrument. First I keep its job small: a specific rubric, pass or fail with a one-line reason, because a one to ten score drifts. I also know the biases. It likes the first answer in a pair, longer answers and its own model family, so for comparisons I swap the order and keep the verdicts that survive it.

Then I measure it against people. Someone labels a gold set, the judge labels the same items, and I look at agreement with Cohen's kappa instead of a raw percentage, because if most items pass, a judge that always says pass looks great on raw agreement. In MockFlow-AI I built an LLM judge for interview verdicts. It had to cite evidence for five competencies, the final verdict was computed in code from those scores, and I checked it against a 50-item human gold set: weighted kappa 0.82. And anything code can decide, I never hand to the judge.
avoid: Reporting raw percent agreement and calling the judge validated.
Using a 1 to 10 score with no rubric anchors and treating the average as a measurement.
Changing the judge model or prompt without re-running it on the gold set.

topics.title: Eval sets, regression and replay
topics.brief: An eval harness is a fixed set of real cases and scorers that you run on every change, so 'is it better?' has a number and 'did it break something?' has an answer.
points: Start from failures, not a benchmark: read real traces, write down how the system fails, and turn each failure into cases. Public benchmarks say little about your product.
Scorers, cheapest first: exact match and rules (valid JSON, the right tool called, the id exists), then an LLM judge for what rules cannot decide, calibrated against a human-labelled sample.

Two kinds of set: capability evals start with a low pass rate and show room to climb; regression evals should sit near 100% so any drop means something broke. A capability case the system passes graduates into the regression set.
Compare old and new on the same cases, per case and per failure class, not only the average. A change can lift one class by 20 points and drop another by 15 while the average barely moves.

One run is a sample: models are non-deterministic. Repeat runs, report pass^k (all k attempts pass) for consistency, and measure the noise floor, how often the same version disagrees with itself, before calling a difference real.
Replay beats invention: re-run recorded production scenarios against the new version, and add every real bug as a case. Sets rot, so a set nobody runs measures nothing.
production: Per Anthropic's engineering post on evals for agents, capability evals start at low pass rates while regression evals should stay near 100%, and mature capability evals are promoted into the regression suite.

Per Hamel Husain's write-up of Rechat's Lucy assistant, evaluation runs at three levels: assertion-style unit tests run often, human and model review of logged traces, and A/B tests as the product matures.
mine: alfred_ (5,000+ active users): I built the eval harness from scratch: production-scenario replay with hybrid deterministic plus LLM-as-judge scoring, catching regressions across 12 failure classes in nightly replays.
MetaRAG (IEEE CAI 2026): an automated evaluation framework behind the 20% fewer hallucinations result, with nine configurations measured against each other.

open.q: How do you know a prompt or model change made things better?
open.probe: Evaluation, from real cases to per-case comparison.
a: Not by trying a few examples: an eval set built from real cases, especially real failures.
Score with deterministic checks where possible and an LLM judge where not.
Run old and new on the same set and compare per case, not only the average.
Every real bug becomes a new case; for a model swap, shadow it on real traffic and blind-judge the disagreements.
An example: the alfred_ eval harness, nightly production-scenario replays across 12 failure classes.

say: Not by trying a few examples and feeling good about it. I built the eval harness at alfred_ from scratch: it replays real production scenarios every night and scores them with deterministic checks plus an LLM judge, across 12 failure classes. Every real bug a user hits becomes a case the next version has to pass.

So a prompt or model change runs against that set before it ships, and I compare per case, which ones got better and which got worse, not only the average. For a model swap I'd go further: run the new model in shadow on real traffic, have a judge compare the disagreements blind, and only then roll it out gradually. That's pretty much the difference between a demo and a product.
avoid: Judging a change by a handful of hand-picked examples.
Reporting only the average, so a regression in one class stays hidden.
Building the set once and never running it again.

topics.title: Online evaluation
topics.brief: An offline set cannot cover everything users do, so you also test on live traffic: shadow a candidate, ramp it, A/B it, then monitor outcomes and drift after it ships.
points: Why online: an offline set only holds cases you thought of, while live traffic brings new inputs, new phrasing and shifting topics. Online signals catch what the set misses and send new cases back into it.
Shadow run: send the candidate the same live requests as production, keep its outputs hidden, and compare. No user risk, but you pay for the extra calls and learn nothing about how users react.

Compare fairly: pair the outputs per request and spend the judge on the disagreements, with the judge blind to which model wrote which and the order randomised. McNemar's test on the discordant pairs, chi^2 = (b - c)^2 / (b + c), says whether one model wins more often than chance.

Ramp, then A/B: serve the candidate to a small cohort first and grow in steps while watching quality, latency and cost, with a rollback trigger agreed in advance. Use an A/B test when you need user outcomes such as completion, edits or retries, randomised by user.

Monitor after launch: sample live traces and score them with the same checks and judge, sliced by cohort, because a flat global average can hide one group getting worse. Watch four kinds of drift: input data, the model (providers update models), retrieval (stale documents) and behaviour.

User signals are noisy but real: thumbs, edits to a draft, retries, escalations to a person. Link each to the trace that produced it and promote failures into the offline set. Watch the monitor too, since a job that has stopped running looks like a quiet week.
production: Per AWS's SageMaker documentation, shadow variants are long-running copies of a candidate that receive production traffic, so you can validate a new component before promoting it.

Per Anthropic's engineering post on evals for agents, production monitoring gives ground truth at scale but is reactive, A/B tests measure real user outcomes but are slow, and the methods work best together.

open.q: You want to replace the model behind a feature with a cheaper one. How do you decide whether to ship it?
open.probe: Offline set, shadow run, fair comparison, gradual rollout and a way back.
a: First the offline set: the candidate has to pass the regression cases and not drop any failure class.
Then a shadow run on real traffic: users only see the old model, and the two outputs are paired per request.
Judge the disagreements blind, with a judge already checked against human labels, and test whether one side wins more than chance.
Ramp a small cohort in steps, with the rollback trigger agreed in advance, watching quality, latency and cost.
Keep monitoring afterwards, sliced by cohort, and feed the failures back into the offline set.

say: I'd treat it like any release, and I wouldn't decide on a benchmark alone. First it has to pass the offline set, the regression cases, without dropping any class. Then I'd run it in shadow on real traffic, so users only ever see the old model's answers, and compare the two outputs request by request. I've done this at alfred_ when we changed the model behind one of our background features: we ran the new model in shadow for a couple of days, then had a judge look at the cases where the two disagreed, without telling it which model wrote which. That judge had been checked against hand labels first.

Only once the disagreements held up did we move a small cohort over, in steps, with a rollback trigger agreed beforehand, and we kept watching the numbers by cohort after that, because a flat average can hide one group getting worse. Anything that went wrong in the live traffic got added back into the offline set. So the model swap is a measured decision, not a hope.
avoid: Shipping a cheaper model because it did well on a public benchmark.
Judging all shadow outputs, or only the matches, instead of the disagreements.
Ramping up with no rollback trigger agreed in advance.

modules.blurb: What changes when an LLM feature meets real users: fewer hallucinations, faster replies, lower cost, visible failures, and how it is added to a product.

topics.title: Reducing hallucinations in production
topics.brief: No single trick removes hallucinations, so layer cheap defences: give the model the facts, limit what it can say, check the output in code, let it abstain, and measure.
points: Ground it: retrieve the facts or call a tool, and tell the model to answer only from them. For long documents, Anthropic's docs add a step: have it pull word-for-word quotes first, then answer from the quotes.
Give it a way out: say what to do when the answer is not there, such as 'I don't have enough information'. A model with no exit fills the gap with the most plausible guess.
Constrain the output: a schema, and options picked from a list your code supplies, so the model chooses an id instead of typing one. Ids and numbers are where it invents most.

Check in code: does the id exist, does the number match the source, is each claim backed by a quote. A grounding check scores the answer against the source and the question, and blocks it below a threshold.
Make the data honest: when a source is incomplete, return that fact with the data (a coverage score), so the model reports the gap instead of smoothing it over.
Measure, and stay humble: replay real failures on every change. These layers reduce hallucinations and never remove them, so keep a hard check or a person in front of anything with consequences.
production: Per AWS's documentation, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails has a contextual grounding check that scores each answer against the source text and the user's question, and blocks answers that fall below a threshold you set.

Per Anthropic's docs on reducing hallucinations, Claude can be told it may say it does not know, asked to extract quotes before answering, and asked to retract any claim it cannot support with a quote.
mine: WheelPrice: a fitment assistant limited to four tools over verified data; each lookup returned a coverage score, and below 0.8 the assistant said the data was partial.
alfred_: re-architected agent memory to ground recall in verified state, cutting fabricated-recall and false-confirmation incidents 80%.
MetaRAG (IEEE CAI 2026): better retrieval alone gave 20% fewer hallucinations than baseline RAG.

a: Ground it: give the model the facts through retrieval or a tool and tell it to answer only from them.

topics.title: Latency: streaming, small models, parallel calls
topics.brief: Users judge speed by the wait before the first useful output, so stream, overlap the stages, keep big models off the critical path and run independent calls in parallel.
points: Know which latency: time to first token (TTFT) is the wait before anything appears. Total time is roughly TTFT plus output tokens times time per token. Streaming fixes the first; shorter outputs and smaller models fix the second.
Stream: send tokens as they arrive, so the screen updates or a voice agent starts speaking before the model has finished writing. The work is the same; the wait feels much shorter.

Overlap the stages: in a voice pipeline, speech-to-text streams partial transcripts to the LLM, the LLM streams tokens to text-to-speech, and audio starts before the answer is complete. What the caller feels is end-of-turn detection plus LLM TTFT plus speech first byte.
Do less per call: shorter prompts, fewer output tokens, and a small fast model on the critical path. Best of all, do not call a model where code can answer.
Parallelize, and avoid chains: independent calls run at the same time. Chained calls add their delays and compound errors. A quick agent can answer while a heavier one works in parallel.
Measure the tail: p95 and p99 are what users remember, so trace every turn to see which stage ate the time. A polling design adds a built-in delay of up to one interval; push or stream instead.
production: Per OpenAI's latency optimization guide, the levers are: process tokens faster, generate fewer tokens, use fewer input tokens, make fewer requests, parallelize, make users wait less, and do not default to an LLM.

Per LiveKit's engineering blog on voice agent architecture, a streaming pipeline overlaps speech-to-text, the LLM and text-to-speech, and the post says sub-one-second end-to-end replies are possible this way.
Per Honeycomb's engineering blog on its Query Assistant, responses took about 2 to 15 seconds, and chaining LLM calls made latency worse and compounded errors.

The lookup, then A, then B
Start the lookup and A together, then run B when A finishes
Run all three one after another to keep it simple
Merge A and B into one prompt in every case
mcq.why: Independent work should overlap. B has to wait for A, but the lookup can run alongside A at no cost to correctness.

mcq.q: Server work is identical, yet a polling design feels slower than streaming. Why?
o: Polling adds up to one interval of waiting, and nothing shows until the full result is ready; streaming shows the start at once
Polling uses a slower protocol for every message
Streaming makes the model faster
Polling forces a smaller context window
Streaming skips the model's safety checks
mcq.why: With polling, a finished result sits until the next poll, and output arrives all at once. Streaming pushes each piece as soon as it exists.

open.q: Users say our AI assistant feels slow. How would you speed it up?
open.probe: Do you measure first, and do you know the levers?
a: Measure first: trace each turn, look at time to first token and the tail percentiles, and find the stage that costs the most.
Stream and overlap stages so the user sees or hears something early.
Cut the work: shorter prompts, fewer output tokens, a smaller model on the critical path, and no model call where code can decide.
Run independent calls in parallel, avoid chains, and cache repeated work.
From my work: MockFlow-AI at sub-400ms with streaming instead of polling; WheelPrice p95 from 1.5s to 300ms.

say: I'd measure before I change anything: trace each request so I can see where the time goes, and look at p95 and p99, not the average, because the tail is what people remember. Then it's usually the same few levers. Stream, so the user sees or hears the start of the answer while the rest is still being written. Cut the work: shorter prompts, fewer output tokens, a smaller model on the critical path, and no model call at all where plain code can decide. And run independent calls in parallel instead of chaining them.

I did this on MockFlow-AI, a voice interview platform. Streaming the speech in, the tokens through and the speech out, instead of polling, got end-to-end latency under 400 milliseconds, about five times faster than a polling baseline. At alfred_ the live voice agent follows the same idea: a light agent gives the quick reply while a heavier one runs in parallel on every turn. And at WheelPrice, query tuning, connection pooling and Redis caching took the API's p95 from 1.5 seconds to 300 milliseconds.
avoid: Saying 'use a faster model' before you know where the time goes.
Quoting the average. The complaint lives in the tail.
Chaining model calls that could run in parallel.

topics.title: Cost: caching, routing, calling the model less
topics.brief: Every model call costs money and time, so cut the number of calls first, the size of each call second, and the price per token third.
points: Call the model only where code cannot decide: exact matches, simple rules and lookups go first, and the model sees only the cases that need judgment about language. This is the biggest saving, and it is also the fastest and easiest path to test.

Prompt caching: providers reuse the already-processed start of a prompt. Put the static part first (tools, system prompt, examples) and the changing part last. Per Anthropic's docs, a cache read is billed at about a tenth of the normal input price, and a cache write costs 25% more for a five-minute cache.

Route and tier: send easy requests to a small cheap model and escalate hard ones. RouteLLM's trained routers cut cost by over 85% on one benchmark while keeping 95% of GPT-4's quality, though those are benchmark numbers, so test on your own traffic.
Batch what is not urgent: batch APIs finish within 24 hours at about half the price. Good for evals, bulk classification and embeddings; wrong for anything a user is waiting on.
Spend fewer tokens: trim context to what the step needs, cap output length, and keep any reasoning budget small where quality allows. Output tokens usually cost more than input tokens.
Measure cost per outcome, not per call: log tokens and spend per feature, cap what one run can spend, and check quality on real traffic. A cheaper path that is wrong costs more later.
production: Per Anthropic's prompt caching docs, cached prefixes are read at a fraction of the base input price, and the default five-minute lifetime refreshes each time the cache is used.
Per the LMSYS blog post on RouteLLM, routing between a strong and a weak model cut costs by over 85% on MT Bench while reaching 95% of GPT-4's performance.
Per OpenAI's Batch API docs, batched requests cost 50% less than synchronous calls and complete within 24 hours.
mine: alfred_: replaced per-message LLM calls in the email-rules engine with a deterministic three-stage matcher, cutting per-user LLM cost 40% at sub-50ms latency with parity match accuracy across 100K+ daily emails.

Cache the model's answers by email subject
Add a cheap deterministic prefilter so the model only sees emails that could plausibly match
Ask the model to answer in fewer tokens
Run the calls in a batch overnight
mcq.why: Most calls are wasted on obvious non-matches. Removing them with plain code beats making each call cheaper, and keeps the model for the genuinely semantic cases.

mcq.q: Every call has a 6,000-token system prompt and a short, changing user question. How should the prompt be ordered to benefit from prompt caching?
o: Static system prompt first, user question last
User question first, system prompt last
Shuffle sections so the cache cannot be gamed
Put the user question in the middle
Order does not matter for caching
mcq.why: Caching matches an identical prefix. Anything that changes early in the prompt breaks the match for everything after it.

mcq.q: A router sends 70% of traffic to a cheap model and spend drops by half, but support tickets start rising. What is the right reading?
o: The saving is real, so keep going
The tickets are unrelated to routing
Raise the temperature of the cheap model
The saving is not proven until quality on the routed traffic is measured, by class, and the escalation rule is tuned
Route 100% to the cheap model
mcq.why: Cost per call fell, but the outcome the customer cares about may have fallen too. Check quality on routed requests, find which classes suffer, and adjust when to escalate.

mcq.q: Which workload fits a batch API with a 24-hour completion window?
o: A live voice call
Re-scoring 100,000 stored support tickets every night
An autocomplete box
A chat reply a user is waiting for
Checking a payment as it is made
mcq.why: Batch trades latency for price. Work that nobody is waiting on is the fit; anything interactive is not.

open.q: How would you keep the LLM cost of a feature down?
open.probe: Do you cut calls before tuning calls, and can you show a measured example?
a: First ask whether a model call is needed: put deterministic code in front and call the model only where code cannot decide.
Cache: the static prompt prefix first, and reuse results for repeated requests, with exact keys rather than embedding similarity alone.
Tier: a small model for easy cases, escalate the rest, and verify on real traffic.
Batch non-urgent work, trim tokens, and cap what one run can spend.
Example: alfred_ email rules, 40% lower LLM cost per user across 100K+ daily emails with parity accuracy.

say: The first question I ask is whether the feature needs a model call at all. At alfred_ the email rules engine used to call the model on every incoming email to check rules. I replaced that with a three-stage matcher: cheap deterministic checks go first, and only the genuinely semantic cases go to the model. That cut LLM cost per user by about 40%, at under 50 milliseconds, with the same match accuracy, across more than 100,000 emails a day.

After that I look at the calls that are left. Put the static part of the prompt first so the provider's prompt cache can reuse it. Send easy requests to a small model and escalate the hard ones, but check that on real traffic, because a cheaper path that's wrong costs more later. Batch anything that isn't urgent, trim the context to what the step needs, and cap what one run can spend. It's also why I measure first: my first guess at where the saving was came from a small test group, and real traffic showed something different.
avoid: Reaching for a cheaper model before asking whether code could decide.
Caching responses on embedding similarity alone: a similar question can need a different answer.
Reporting savings from a small test group without checking real traffic.

topics.title: Observability and incidents
topics.brief: Trace every call and step so a vague complaint becomes a replayable record, and watch outcomes, because a green dashboard can mean a job never delivered anything.
points: Trace, do not only log: a trace links one request's steps (retrieval, each model call, each tool call) with inputs, outputs, tokens, latency and cost. A bad answer becomes a record you can open and replay.

Watch the basics plus LLM extras: latency (including p95 and p99), traffic, errors and saturation, which Google's SRE book calls the four golden signals. For LLM apps add cost per request, token counts, cache hit rate and a quality score from sampled online evals.

Alert on symptoms, debug with causes: page when users are hurt (answers late, wrong or missing), then use traces to find why. 'Job succeeded' is a statement about the job runner, not about the outcome.
An absent run is a failure: a job that should run every hour and has not run is as broken as one that errored. Keep a run ledger and alert when an expected run is missing.
Providers change under you: models get retired and updated. If errors are swallowed, a retired model fails silently, so alert on dead models, empty results and a rise in fallbacks.
Incident order: stop the harm (roll back or turn the flag off), scope from evidence, change one thing at a time, then write it up and add the alert that would have caught it.
production: Per Anthropic's engineering post on its multi-agent research system, adding full production tracing let the team diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically, while watching decision patterns without reading individual conversations.
Per Google's SRE book, monitoring should page on symptoms and use cause-based signals mainly for debugging, and the four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
mine: alfred_: owns the reliability layer of the multi-agent assistant, including an eval harness built from scratch that replays production scenarios nightly with hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-judge scoring across 12 failure classes.
alfred_: found scheduled jobs failing behind green dashboards, and moved monitoring from job status to delivered outcomes.

The scheduler's step ran, such as queuing the work, and says nothing about delivery
The dashboard is showing the wrong date
The job ran twice
The model returned a long answer

o: Alert on any error log line
Alert when error rate exceeds 5%
Alert when latency rises
Alert when an expected run is missing, using a ledger of runs
Add more retries
mcq.why: A job that never starts produces no errors and no latency. Only a check against the expected schedule notices the absence.

mcq.q: A user reports 'the assistant gave me a wrong answer yesterday'. What makes this debuggable?
o: A stored trace of that request: inputs, retrieved context, tool calls and outputs
A bigger model
A lower temperature
A new system prompt
The user's description of what they asked
mcq.why: Without the exact context and steps you are guessing. A trace lets you replay the request and see whether retrieval, a tool or the model went wrong.

mcq.q: A cron-driven feature starts returning empty results every run after the provider retires the model it uses. The code catches the error and returns an empty list. What did monitoring miss?
o: The server's CPU load
The size of the prompt
The cost per call
The cache hit rate
Swallowed errors: nothing alerted on dead models, empty results or error rate per model
mcq.why: Catching an error and returning something plausible hides a total outage. Alert on error rate by model and on unusual emptiness, not only on crashes.

open.q: Your AI feature breaks in production and you have an hour to fix it, with AI tools allowed. How do you work?
open.probe: Debugging under pressure without handing the thinking to the tool.
a: Stop the damage first: roll back or turn the flag off if a recent change is the likely cause.
Scope it from evidence: when it started, what changed, who is affected, from traces, logs and metrics.
Use AI for fast, checkable work such as summarising a log or explaining a stack trace, and verify each answer against the system.
The cause and the fix stay mine; change one thing at a time and measure.
Afterwards, a write-up and an alert so it cannot fail silently, as with crons that were failing behind green dashboards.

say: First I'd stop the damage: if something shipped recently, roll it back or turn the flag off, and fix forward later. Then scope it from evidence, when it started, what changed at that time, who's affected, from the traces and metrics, not from a guess.

I'd use AI for the parts that are fast to check: summarising a huge log, explaining a stack trace in code I don't know, drafting a query. But every answer gets checked against the real system, because under pressure is exactly when a confident wrong answer costs the most. The cause and the fix stay my call, one change at a time. Afterwards, a short write-up and an alert so it can't fail silently again. I learned that one the hard way at alfred_, with crons that were failing behind green dashboards: the scheduler said 'succeeded' because the work had been queued, not because anything was delivered. So I watch the outcome now, not the job status, and a run that should have happened and didn't counts as a failure.
avoid: Fixing forward when a rollback is available and the cause is unknown.
Pasting logs into an AI tool and acting on the answer without checking it against the system.
Saying 'we have dashboards' without saying what they would have caught.

topics.title: Adding AI to a product
topics.brief: Start from the customer problem, use code or search where they solve it, use the model for judgment on language, and ship small with a fallback and a measure of the outcome.
points: Work backwards from the customer: a task that is slow, repetitive or hard to search. Write down what they do today and what better looks like before you choose a model.
Code first: if rules, search or a lookup solves it, use them. Use a model for the part that needs judgment on language and keep the rest deterministic.
Build the eval set before the feature: collect real examples, define 'good' in writing, score. Without it you cannot tell a better version from a worse one.
Constrain the first version: limited tools, verified data, output the user can edit, and nothing destructive. Start simple and add complexity only when the data says to.

Roll out small: a flag, a small group, a kill switch and a fallback so the product still works when the model is slow or wrong. Measure the outcome the customer cares about (tickets, time saved, suggestions accepted), not model scores.

Expect the usual traps, from Chip Huyen's list: using generative AI where it is not needed, blaming the AI for a bad product, starting too complex, trusting early success, and skipping human evaluation.
production: Per GitHub's engineering blog, Copilot began as a chat prototype and was moved into the editor because it proved useful in almost every situation there; GitHub used acceptance rate and characters retained to judge whether extra context helped.

Per Honeycomb's engineering blog, its Query Assistant turns a question into a query the user can refine, was built in about a month with scope cut hard, and used non-destructive output, output validation, no chat UI and per-user rate limits against prompt injection.
mine: WheelPrice: an embeddable fitment assistant limited to four tools over verified data, built to cut fitment-related support tickets.
MockFlow-AI: a live voice interview platform where code owns the interview flow and the model only phrases each move.

When the input is messy
When a user is waiting
When rules or a lookup solve it accurately, as with fitment checked against a table

open.q: How would you add AI to an existing product?
open.probe: Customer Obsession: do you start from the problem and the outcome, not the model?
a: Start from a customer problem that is slow, repetitive or hard to search, not from the model.
Ask whether code or search solves it first; use the model where judgment on language is needed.
Build an eval set from real examples before the feature.
Ship to a small group behind a flag with a fallback, and measure the outcome the customer cares about.
Example: the WheelPrice assistant answered from verified product data through tools, and said so when the data was partial.

say: I'd start from the customer, not the model: where are people spending time on something repetitive, or struggling to find something? Then I'd ask whether plain code or search solves it first, and use the model only where you actually need judgment on language.

Before building, I'd collect real examples and turn them into an eval set, so we know what good looks like. Then ship it to a small group behind a flag, with a fallback so the product still works when the model is slow or wrong, and measure the outcome the customer cares about. At WheelPrice the customer assistant answered from our verified product data through tools, never from the model's memory, because a wrong fitment answer costs the customer money, and when the data for a car was only partly there, it said so.
avoid: Starting from 'we should use an LLM' instead of from a customer problem.
Launching to everyone with no flag, no fallback and no eval set.
Reporting model scores as success instead of the customer outcome.

modules.title: 7. Fine-tuning
modules.blurb: When to tune instead of prompting or retrieving, and how LoRA makes tuning cheap.

topics.title: Fine-tune, RAG or prompt?
topics.brief: Prompt first, add retrieval when the model lacks facts, and fine-tune when you need a behaviour, a format or a cheaper model that prompting cannot reach.
points: The ladder: write evals, then prompt (clear instructions, examples), then add retrieval for missing knowledge, then fine-tune for behaviour. Each step costs more to build and maintain than the one before.
Prompt when the model can already do the task and you need to steer it. It is the fastest to change and needs no data beyond a few examples.
RAG when the answer depends on facts that are private, fresh or need a citation. The facts stay in your data, so updating a document updates the answer.

Fine-tune when you need a consistent format or style, a narrow skill, shorter prompts, or a smaller cheaper model doing one task. You train on examples of the exact input and output you want; AWS suggests starting with 50 to 100 high-quality ones.

Fine-tuning is a poor way to add knowledge: one study found models learn new facts slowly that way and, once learned, those examples raise hallucination; another found RAG beat fine-tuning for old and new knowledge.

Fine-tuning has upkeep: the tuned model is tied to its base model, so you re-train and re-evaluate when the base changes or the data drifts. Decide with your own eval, not a rule of thumb. The approaches also combine: tune for style, retrieve for facts.
production: Per OpenAI's model optimization guide, the flow is evals first, then prompting, and fine-tuning only for some use cases, such as consistent formatting, shorter prompts, or a smaller cheaper model for one task.

Per AWS's announcement, Amazon Bedrock lets you fine-tune Claude 3 Haiku on your own labelled examples for classification, structured output and tool use, and advises starting with 50 to 100 high-quality rows.
Per the same OpenAI guide, fine-tuned models stay available for inference only until their base models are deprecated, which is the upkeep cost in one sentence.
mine: MetaRAG (IEEE CAI 2026, first author): improved answers by changing retrieval, not the model: 82.5% precision and 20% fewer hallucinations than baseline RAG.
alfred_: replaced per-message LLM calls in the email-rules engine with a deterministic three-stage matcher, cutting per-user LLM cost 40% at parity accuracy: sometimes the cheapest rung is no model.
WheelPrice: fine-tuned a YOLO model to locate wheels in photos for a fitment visualizer (a vision model, not an LLM).

Add a multi-agent vote
Increase the temperature
mcq.why: This is a behaviour problem at scale. A small tuned model can learn the task without the long prompt, cutting cost and latency. Test it against the current setup on your eval.

o: The learning rate was too low; train longer on the same data
The model is too small; fine-tune a bigger one on the same facts
Fine-tuning is poor at adding facts and can raise hallucination; use retrieval for the facts and check with evals
Temperature is too high; set it to zero
The documents need to be shorter
mcq.why: Studies find new facts are learned slowly through fine-tuning and then increase hallucination. Keep facts in retrieval and use tuning for behaviour.

mcq.q: Which is a good reason NOT to fine-tune yet?
o: You have no eval set, so you cannot tell whether the tuned model is better
You want a consistent JSON format
You want a smaller model for one narrow task
Your prompts are long and repeated on every call
You have thousands of labelled examples
mcq.why: Without an eval you cannot measure a gain or catch a regression. The other options are the situations where fine-tuning is worth testing.

open.q: When would you fine-tune a model instead of using RAG or better prompts?
open.probe: A decision ladder with reasons, and honesty about experience.
a: Climb a ladder with evals from the start: prompt, then RAG, then fine-tune.
RAG for knowledge that is private, fresh or needs a citation; updating a document updates the answer.
Fine-tune for behaviour: a strict format, a style, a narrow skill, shorter prompts, or a smaller cheaper model.
Not for adding facts: models learn them slowly and it can raise hallucination; RAG beat it in comparisons.
Upkeep, and an example with a number: MetaRAG's 20% fewer hallucinations came from retrieval, not tuning.

say: I'd go up a ladder, and start with evals so I can tell whether a step helped. First, a better prompt with a few examples. If the model is missing facts, because they're private, change often, or need a source, I add retrieval. Only if the problem is behaviour that prompting can't fix do I consider fine-tuning: a strict output format, a style, a narrow task, or getting a smaller, cheaper model to do one job well. Fine-tuning is a poor way to add knowledge. Research shows models learn new facts slowly that way and it can raise hallucinations, and retrieval did better in the comparisons.

Fine-tuning also has upkeep: you retrain and re-evaluate when the base model changes or the data drifts, so I'd want a measured gap first. Most of my experience is on the other rungs. In MetaRAG I got about twenty percent fewer hallucinations than baseline RAG by improving retrieval, and at alfred_ I cut per-user LLM cost forty percent by replacing per-message model calls with a deterministic matcher. I did fine-tune a YOLO model at WheelPrice, which is vision, but the lesson was the same: start with the cheapest thing that the eval says works.
avoid: Saying fine-tuning teaches the model your documents: it teaches behaviour, and facts are better kept in retrieval.
Reaching for fine-tuning before you have an eval set to prove it helped.

topics.title: LoRA and parameter-efficient tuning
topics.brief: LoRA freezes the base model and trains two small matrices beside each chosen weight, so a task adapter is tiny to train, store and swap, and costs nothing extra at inference once merged.
points: The idea: instead of updating a big weight matrix W (d x k), train a low-rank update. The layer computes W'x = Wx + (alpha / r) B A x, with B (d x r) and A (r x k). Only A and B train; W stays frozen.

The numbers: for d = k = 4096 and r = 8, A and B hold 8 x (4096 + 4096) = 65,536 parameters against 16.8 million in W, about 0.4%. The LoRA paper reports about 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and 3 times less GPU memory than full fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B.

Setup: B starts at zero, so training begins from the base model's behaviour. The rank r sets capacity (8 or 16 are common) and alpha scales the update. Apply it to all layers, MLPs included: at the same parameter count, attention-only LoRA does worse.
Inference: merge W + (alpha / r) B A into one matrix and there is no added latency, or keep adapters separate and swap them per request on one base model.

QLoRA: keep the frozen base in 4-bit (NormalFloat) and train LoRA adapters on top, with paged optimizers. It fine-tuned a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU. Raschka measured about 33% less memory for about 39% more training time, with little change in quality.

Limits: LoRA matches full fine-tuning on small to medium datasets, but falls behind when the data exceeds its capacity (low ranks hit this sooner) and at large batch sizes. Its best learning rate is about 10x the full fine-tuning one. Like any fine-tune, it teaches behaviour better than facts.
production: Per Apple's foundation models report, Apple Intelligence trains small LoRA adapters (rank 16, tens of megabytes for the roughly 3B on-device model) for tasks such as summarization, and loads and swaps them on the fly over one frozen base model.
Per vLLM's documentation, one server can serve many LoRA adapters on a single base model, chosen per request by putting the adapter's name in the model field.
mine: Quantization in production: an INT8 TorchScript audio inference service at 150ms p95 for assistant-patient voice interaction (UIC VARE Lab), the serving side of the same memory-versus-quality trade-off.
WheelPrice: fine-tuned a YOLO model to locate wheels in photos for a fitment visualizer.

open.q: What is LoRA and why would you use it?
open.probe: The mechanism with the parameter math, and the limits.
a: Freeze the pretrained weights and train a low-rank update beside them: W + (alpha / r) B A.
The math: r(d + k) parameters instead of d x k; about 0.4% for r = 8 and a 4096-wide layer.
B starts at zero; merge for no inference latency, or keep adapters separate and swap them per request.
QLoRA: 4-bit frozen base plus adapters; 65B on one 48 GB GPU, about a third less memory for about 39% more time.
Limits: behaviour not facts, capacity on very large datasets; apply to all layers.

say: LoRA is a way to fine-tune a big model without updating all of its weights. You freeze the pretrained weights, and next to a weight matrix you train two small matrices, A and B, whose product is a low-rank update. The rank is small, often eight or sixteen, so for a four-thousand-wide layer you train about sixty-five thousand numbers instead of sixteen million. B starts at zero, so training begins from the base model's behaviour, and after training you can merge the update into the weights, so there's no extra latency at inference.

That makes it cheap to train, and an adapter is tiny, so one base model can serve many tasks by swapping adapters, which is what Apple does on device. QLoRA goes further: keep the frozen base in 4-bit and train the adapters on top, which got a 65-billion-parameter model onto one 48 GB GPU. The catch is the usual one with fine-tuning: it's good for behaviour, format and narrow tasks, not for adding facts, and it can fall behind full fine-tuning on a very large dataset. On my side I know the quantization half from serving: at UIC I deployed an INT8 audio model at 150 milliseconds p95.
avoid: Saying LoRA makes inference faster or compresses the model: it cuts training cost, and once merged, inference is unchanged.
Saying LoRA adds knowledge reliably: like any fine-tune it shapes behaviour, and facts belong in retrieval.

points: Situation: the tool, the task, why you used it.

Candidates: a deep research run where a second, checking pass refuted 17 of 18 claims from the first; a coding agent reporting a test passed or a function existed when it did not.
